title: NASA: LOST MISSIONS
subtitle: Opportunity RPG Mission

story_arc.opening: Opportunity was sent to Meridiani Planum to investigate rocks and soils shaped by ancient water.
story_arc.turn: The rover kept exploring for almost 15 years and traveled 45.16 kilometers, far beyond its planned 90 sols.
story_arc.ending: A planet-wide dust storm darkened the sky. Opportunity's last signal arrived on June 10, 2018, as the rover struggled to make energy.
story_arc.emotional_line: Its final message was not a farewell speech: it was a dark, incomplete image sent through the storm.

hardware.name: Opportunity (MER-B)
hardware.what_it_was: A solar-powered robotic geologist equipped with cameras, a robotic arm and rock-analysis instruments.
hardware.why_sent: To study Martian rocks and soil for evidence of past water and environments that may once have been habitable.
hardware.instrument: Panoramic Camera, APXS, Microscopic Imager and Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT)
hardware.discovery: Opportunity found hematite-rich spheres nicknamed blueberries and other evidence that liquid water shaped ancient Mars.
hardware.why_left: A planet-wide dust storm reduced sunlight reaching its solar panels. After months of recovery attempts, NASA ended the mission in 2019.
hardware.what_remains: The rover remains in Perseverance Valley at the edge of Endeavour Crater. Its instruments and structure are still there; the images and data it sent are preserved in NASA's archives on Earth.

current_status.location: Perseverance Valley, edge of Endeavour Crater, Mars
current_status.last_event: Last communication: June 10, 2018. NASA declared the mission complete: February 13, 2019.

gallery.title: Meridiani from Opportunity's eyes
gallery.kid_text: This is real Mars terrain seen by Opportunity. The rover was not just driving: it was looking for clues in rocks and soil.

gallery.title: Opportunity's self-portrait
gallery.kid_text: Opportunity built this self-portrait from many camera images while it worked on Mars, giving a real view of the rover in the field.

gallery.title: Martian "blueberries" on the ground
gallery.kid_text: Opportunity found round, iron-rich spheres nicknamed blueberries. Scientists studied them as clues that liquid water once shaped Meridiani Planum.

gallery.title: Rover landing hardware at Eagle Crater
gallery.kid_text: From orbit, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted Opportunity's landing hardware in Eagle Crater, where the mission began on Mars.

gallery.title: Opportunity's final traverse map
gallery.kid_text: This map shows the long route Opportunity drove across Mars and where it was working in Perseverance Valley when contact was lost.

gallery.title: Opportunity's last message
gallery.kid_text: This noisy, incomplete image taken on June 10, 2018 was the last data Opportunity sent back during the global dust storm.

sample_facts.text: Opportunity’s RAT tool brushed rock surfaces so its instruments could examine fresh material underneath.
Opportunity’s Mini-TES identified minerals from a distance using infrared measurements.
Opportunity’s APXS measured the chemical composition of rocks and soil.
The Microscopic Imager helped Opportunity inspect tiny textures on Martian rocks and soil.
Opportunity used its cameras to build panoramas and document the places it explored.

dialogue.intro_npc_1: Welcome, R.O.M. Meridiani Planum is full of round stones that look like tiny blueberries.
dialogue.intro_npc_2: Find Opportunity, sort the mineral clues, and discover why scientists connected this place with ancient water.
dialogue.npc_hint: Look for the rover, the geology sorter, dark-blue spheres, and the solar panel station.
dialogue.npc_first_hint: Opportunity is north-east of here. Walk next to it and press A.
dialogue.rover_before_npc: A quiet rover rests in the dust. Maybe Dr. Vega can help you understand it.
dialogue.rover_intro: Opportunity (MER-B) launched on July 7, 2003 and landed in Meridiani Planum on January 25, 2004 (UTC; January 24, 2004 PST).
dialogue.rover_after_id: Correct. Opportunity lasted almost 15 years, far beyond its planned 90 sols.
dialogue.rover_waiting: Opportunity is still quiet. You need mineral evidence and the final dust-storm clue.
dialogue.case_locked: A geology sorter is offline. First identify the rover so you know what the samples mean.
dialogue.case_open: You found the geology sorter. New skill unlocked: Mineral Classification.
dialogue.case_fact: Opportunity used instruments including APXS, the Microscopic Imager and the RAT to study rocks and soil.
dialogue.dish: The solar panel station is a simulation of the engineering problem. It can help you understand why Opportunity's signal weakened.
dialogue.panel: SIMULATION: During a global dust storm, less sunlight could reach Opportunity's solar panels. The real rover's historical ending cannot be changed here.
dialogue.soil_locked: A field of round stones. You need the geology sorter before classifying them.
dialogue.soil_done: You already recorded this mineral clue.
dialogue.soil_fact: Opportunity found hematite-rich spheres, nicknamed blueberries, in Meridiani Planum. NASA explains that these minerals are clues to liquid water in Mars' past.
dialogue.soil_good: Good. The rounded spheres are now part of your evidence log.
dialogue.nothing: Nothing to inspect here. Try people, machines, tools, samples, or the solar station.

final_clues.text: SIMULATION CLUE: A Mars-wide dust storm darkened the sky and reduced sunlight reaching Opportunity's solar panels.
CLUE #02: Opportunity's solar-powered systems had less energy available while the storm continued.
CLUE #03: Opportunity's last signal was heard on June 10, 2018; NASA declared the mission complete on February 13, 2019.

storm.start: Dust event! The sky turns orange and the rover's solar energy drops.
storm.fact: NASA reported that a historic Mars-wide dust storm reduced the energy available to Opportunity's solar panels.
storm.success: SIMULATION COMPLETE: You explored the power problem. In the historical record, Opportunity still stopped communicating during the storm.

ending.title: You discovered the story of Opportunity.
ending.tagline: They were left behind. Their stories weren't.
ending.codex_text: Opportunity complete: planned for 90 sols, operated for almost 15 years, traveled 45.16 kilometers, and helped reveal that liquid water shaped Mars in the past. Its last signal was a dark, incomplete image sent during a planet-wide dust storm.
